subject: Geography
sub_topic: Coastal plains — east vs west coast comparison

concepts.name: Width and Extent of Coastal Plains: East vs West
key_dimensions: West coast is narrower (10–25 km) vs East coast is wider (100–130 km) — and why
Role of Western Ghats proximity in constraining the west coast width
Eastern Coastal Plain as a wider depositional plain formed by eastward-flowing rivers
UPSC trap: Exceptions where the west coast widens (e.g., Gujarat coast/Kathiawar region)

concepts.name: Formation Mechanisms: Submerged vs Emergent Coasts
key_dimensions: West coast as a submerged/drowned coastline — ria coast theory and tectonic subsidence
East coast as an emergent coastline — uplift and marine regression
Geomorphological signatures: West has estuaries/backwaters, East has deltas/lagoons
UPSC trap: Distinguishing 'drowned coast' features (fjords, rias) from 'emergent coast' features (beaches, sandbars)

concepts.name: River Behavior on East vs West Coasts
key_dimensions: West coast rivers: Short, swift, non-navigable, no delta formation due to steep gradient
East coast rivers: Long, slow, navigable, form extensive deltas (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri)
Why western rivers drain into the Arabian Sea despite the Western Ghats being the watershed
UPSC trap: Tapi and Narmada are exceptions — flow west through rift valleys, not typical west-coast rivers

concepts.name: Delta Formation on the East Coast: Types and Significance
key_dimensions: Major deltas: Mahanadi, Godavari (largest active delta), Krishna, Kaveri — characteristics and differences
Conditions favouring delta formation: shallow continental shelf, low wave energy, sediment-rich rivers
Absence of deltas on the west coast and why (high wave energy, short rivers, steep gradient)
UPSC trap: Godavari delta is the largest on east coast; Krishna-Godavari delta is a combined/shared delta system

concepts.name: Backwaters (Kayals) of the West Coast
key_dimensions: Definition, formation mechanism — wave action creating sand bars, trapping seawater
Kerala's Vembanad Lake as the largest backwater; Ashtamudi Kyal
Economic significance: fishing, tourism, inland navigation (National Waterway 3)
UPSC trap: Chilika Lake (east coast) is a lagoon, NOT a backwater — distinction between lagoon and backwater

concepts.name: Lagoons and Lake Systems of the East Coast
key_dimensions: Chilika Lake: largest brackish water lagoon in Asia, location, ecological significance (Ramsar site)
Pulicat Lake: second largest brackish water lagoon, straddles Andhra Pradesh–Tamil Nadu border
Formation: longshore drift and sandbars separating shallow water from the sea
UPSC trap: Chilika is in Odisha (not Andhra Pradesh); Pulicat's Sriharikota Island (ISRO launch site) is its sandbar

concepts.name: Subdivisions of the West Coast: North to South
key_dimensions: Konkan Coast (Maharashtra–Goa), Kanara/Karnataka Coast, Malabar Coast (Kerala)
Gujarat coast / Kathiawar as an atypical northern extension with different geomorphology
Malabar Coast: maximum backwater development, highest rainfall, specific vegetation
UPSC trap: The term 'Coromandel' is east coast; 'Malabar' is west coast — frequently confused in options

concepts.name: Subdivisions of the East Coast: North to South
key_dimensions: Northern Circar / Utkal Plains (Odisha), Andhra Coast (Krishna-Godavari deltaic), Coromandel Coast (Tamil Nadu)
Coromandel Coast: receives rain from northeast monsoon (unique reversal compared to rest of India)
Utkal Plains: known for deltaic plains and temple towns (Puri, Bhubaneswar proximity)
UPSC trap: Coromandel Coast gets winter rainfall from retreating/NE monsoon — a major UPSC favourite

concepts.name: Rainfall Pattern Differences: East vs West Coast
key_dimensions: West coast: receives Southwest monsoon rainfall (June–September), among the highest in India (Malabar coast)
East coast: receives Northeast monsoon (October–December), especially Coromandel Coast
Chennai receives most of its rainfall from NE monsoon, not SW monsoon — a classic UPSC trap
Leeward side effect: East coast in rain shadow during SW monsoon but compensated by NE monsoon

concepts.name: Continental Shelf Differences and Maritime Significance
key_dimensions: East coast has a wider, shallower continental shelf — supports richer fisheries and delta building
West coast has a narrower continental shelf but significant offshore oil/gas reserves (Mumbai High)
Wider shelf on east = more favourable for port development via natural harbours vs artificial ports on west
UPSC trap: Mumbai High is an offshore oil field on the WEST coast continental shelf — frequently misattributed

concepts.name: Natural Harbours: East vs West Coast Comparison
key_dimensions: West coast has more natural harbours due to submerged coastline (Mumbai, Kandla, Marmagao, Kochi)
East coast lacks natural deep harbours due to straight, emergent coastline — ports are mostly artificial
Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, Ennore (Kamarajar) are artificial/semi-artificial ports
UPSC trap: Visakhapatnam has a natural harbour — one of the few exceptions on the east coast

concepts.name: Mangrove Ecosystems: Distribution and Comparison
key_dimensions: Sundarbans (West Bengal/East Coast) — largest mangrove forest in the world; UNESCO and Ramsar site
Bhitarkanika (Odisha) — second largest mangrove in India, often confused with Sundarbans
West coast mangroves: fragmented, less extensive (Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu; Coondapur in Karnataka)
UPSC trap: Pichavaram is on the EAST coast (Tamil Nadu), not west coast — a common confusion point

concepts.name: Soil Types on Coastal Plains
key_dimensions: Alluvial soils on east coast deltaic plains — highly fertile, supports intensive agriculture (rice bowl regions)
Laterite soils on west coast (especially Kerala, Karnataka) — leached, less fertile, suitable for plantation crops
Coastal sandy soils (teri soils in Tamil Nadu) — unique reddish sandy soils of south Tamil Nadu coast
UPSC trap: 'Teri soils' are specific to the southeastern coast, not the west — highly niche but asked in Prelims

concepts.name: Cyclone Vulnerability: East vs West Coast
key_dimensions: East coast is far more cyclone-prone (Bay of Bengal generates ~80% of global tropical cyclones)
Reasons: Bay of Bengal retains higher sea surface temperatures, enclosed geometry, slower storm dissipation
West coast: Arabian Sea cyclones are fewer but have been intensifying (Cyclone Biparjoy, Tauktae as recent examples)
UPSC trap: Arabian Sea cyclone frequency is rising due to climate change — a contemporary angle for Mains

concepts.name: Coastal Erosion and Accretion Patterns
key_dimensions: East coast faces higher erosion due to cyclones, longshore drift, and delta subsidence
Sea-level rise threat disproportionately impacts low-lying east coast deltaic plains
West coast erosion: localized, aggravated by sand mining from rivers and coastal construction
UPSC trap: Longshore drift moves sediment southward along east coast — affects Pulicat and river mouth dynamics

concepts.name: Ports and Economic Geography of Coastal Plains
key_dimensions: Major ports on west coast: Mumbai (JNPT), Kandla (Deendayal), Kochi, New Mangalore, Marmagao
Major ports on east coast: Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, Kamarajar (Ennore), Haldia
Sagarmala Project and coastal economic zones — differential development east vs west
UPSC trap: Kandla (Deendayal Port) is India's largest port by cargo volume, not Mumbai — frequently tested

concepts.name: Estuaries on the West Coast vs Deltas on the East Coast
key_dimensions: Estuaries form where rivers meet sea in funnel shape — west coast (Narmada, Tapi form estuaries, not deltas)
Why Narmada and Tapi form estuaries: hard rock, rift valley, tidal action dominant, limited sediment deposition
Contrast with east coast rivers that deposit sediment on gentle slopes forming prograding deltas
UPSC trap: Narmada is a major west-flowing river forming an ESTUARY — not a delta — classic Prelims trap

concepts.name: Coral Reef Systems near Indian Coasts
key_dimensions: Gulf of Mannar (east coast/southeastern) and Lakshadweep (west coast/Arabian Sea) — major reef systems
Andaman & Nicobar coral reefs — threatened by bleaching (1998 El Niño event reference)
Gulf of Kutch (west coast) — fringing reefs, northernmost coral reefs of India
UPSC trap: Lakshadweep atolls are coral islands (west), not to be confused with Andaman (volcanic/east) — fundamental distinction

concepts.name: Tidal Phenomena and Tidal Ports on the Coasts
key_dimensions: Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay) on west coast: among highest tidal range in India — tidal power potential
Kandla port is a tidal port — ships enter only during high tide
East coast: relatively lower tidal range, more stable port operations
UPSC trap: Tidal energy potential sites in India are primarily on the WEST coast (Gulf of Khambhat, Gulf of Kutch), not east coast

concepts.name: Coastal Plains and Agricultural Systems
key_dimensions: East coast deltaic plains: intensive paddy cultivation (Krishna-Godavari delta called 'Rice Bowl of India')
West coast: plantation agriculture — rubber, coconut, spices, cashew due to laterite soils and high rainfall
Aquaculture and fisheries: prawn farming concentrated in east coast deltas; sardine/mackerel fisheries on west coast
UPSC trap: 'Rice Bowl of India' refers to multiple regions — Andhra Pradesh (east coast deltas) most commonly, but Chhattisgarh also claims it
